rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Injection 1 already reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient at unchanged temperature to seek a faster fully resolved method and measure how the critical pairs respond to slope.

The six-minute gradient retains full resolution with a minimum R of 2.46. Test the next shorter grid duration to reduce analysis time while checking whether the early critical pair remains above R = 1.5.

The four-minute gradient reaches maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for the first pair. Raise temperature at unchanged gradient to test whether faster elution and a selectivity shift can preserve full resolution.

Heating worsened the early critical pair, so test the lowest temperature to improve its selectivity while shortening the gradient to the minimum duration. This probes whether cooling can offset the resolution loss from a steeper gradient; injection 3 remains the fastest validated maximum-score method.

Reduce the gradient slope at the minimum duration to raise the early pair’s resolution from 1.23 toward 1.5. The last compound will likely elute during the final hold, so this tests whether full resolution can be restored while remaining faster than injection 3.

Shift the successful two-minute gradient window upward while preserving its slope. The stronger endpoint should accelerate the last compound substantially; this run checks whether the higher starting fraction preserves resolution of the early pair.

Shift the window upward another 0.10 at unchanged slope and temperature to accelerate the last peak and reduce its hold time. The preceding shift preserved early-pair resolution, but this run will check for loss of initial retention.

Increase the starting fraction by one grid step to shorten elution further while making the gradient slightly shallower. Check the early pair carefully because its first peak is approaching the weakly retained region.

Use the early pair’s increased resolution margin to test a one-step temperature increase, which should accelerate the last peak. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate whether the temperature-induced selectivity loss remains acceptable.

Test whether a higher starting fraction can shorten the run while the shallower gradient preserves early-pair resolution. Return to 25 C for its better selectivity, since the first peak may now approach the unretained region.

Return to the fastest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature one more step to locate its resolution boundary. The early pair may fall below 1.5, but this directly tests whether further time savings are possible without sacrificing maximum CRF.

Reduce the endpoint by one grid step to soften the gradient and try to recover the early pair’s resolution at 35 C. This tests whether the temperature-driven time savings can offset the weaker final solvent; injection 10 remains the fastest validated maximum-score method.

Lower the starting fraction to keep the early pair retained and return to 30 C, where selectivity was adequate. This tests a slightly slower alternative to injection 10 that may provide more resolution margin while retaining maximum CRF.

Combine the best-tested starting fraction with a slightly shallower gradient at the temperature favoring early-pair selectivity. This should provide more resolution margin than injection 10 while keeping the last peak near three minutes and preserving maximum CRF.

Test the intermediate temperature for the narrowed gradient, bracketed by full resolution at 25 C and an early-pair failure at 35 C. This may shorten injection 15 while retaining more resolution margin than the fastest validated method, injection 10.

Test a shallower two-minute gradient with a lower starting fraction to increase early-pair resolution and retention. Maximum CRF is already secured; this explores a larger resolution margin at the cost of a modestly longer final hold.

Raise temperature one step from injection 17 to shorten the final hold while using its early-pair resolution margin. Injection 10 remains the fastest maximum-CRF method; this tests an alternative with stronger initial retention.

Test the intermediate endpoint between injections 8 and 17 to balance early-pair resolution against final-hold duration. This should preserve maximum CRF with stronger initial retention than injection 10, which remains the fastest validated method.

Lower the starting fraction from injection 8 to strengthen initial retention while retaining the strongest endpoint and minimum gradient duration. This tests whether the early pair remains fully resolved with little change in last-peak time; injection 10 remains the fastest validated maximum-score method.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 20 to improve its marginal early-pair resolution while preserving initial retention. This should retain maximum CRF with only a modest increase in final-hold time; injection 10 remains the fastest validated fully resolved method.

Test the remaining nearby high-endpoint method to determine whether stronger initial retention than injection 10 can coexist with full resolution at 30 C. The early pair is near its expected resolution boundary; injection 10 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF method.

Extend the endpoint refinement from injection 15 to seek additional early-pair resolution margin while keeping the minimum gradient duration. Maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 10 remains the fastest validated fully resolved method.

Raise temperature one step from injection 23 to shorten the final hold while retaining its improved early-pair resolution margin. Injection 10 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF method; this tests the warmer version of the more resolved alternative.

Use the final injection to refine the fully resolved method from injection 21: a one-step lower endpoint should improve early-pair resolution while keeping all peaks well within ten minutes. Maximum CRF is already achieved, and injection 10 remains the fastest validated fully resolved method.
